'''''Beyond Infinity : An Expedition to the Outer Limits of Mathematics''''' is a [[popular mathematics]] book by [[Eugenia Cheng]] centered on concepts of [[infinity]]. It was published by [[Basic Books]] and (with a slightly different title) by [[Profile Books]] in 2017,{{r|simoson|bultheel|haworth}} and in a paperback edition in 2018.{{r|guadarrama}} It was shortlisted for the [[Royal Society Prizes for Science Books|2017 Royal Society Insight Investment Science Book Prize]].{{r|roysoc}}

==Topics==
The book is divided into two parts, with the first exploring notions leading to concepts of [[actual infinity]], concrete but infinite mathematical values. After an exploration of [[number system]]s, this part discusses [[set theory]], [[cardinal number]]s, and [[ordinal number]]s, [[transfinite arithmetic]], and the existence of different infinite sizes of sets. Topics used to illustrate these concepts include [[Hilbert's paradox of the Grand Hotel]], [[Cantor's diagonal argument]],{{r|guadarrama}} and the unprovability of the [[continuum hypothesis]].{{r|bultheel}}

The second part concerns mathematics related to the idea of [[potential infinity]], the assignment of finite values to the results of infinite processes including [[Asymptotic analysis|growth rates]], [[Limit (mathematics)|limits]], and [[series (mathematics)|infinite series]].{{r|guadarrama|bultheel}} This part also discusses [[Zeno's paradoxes]], [[Dedekind cut]]s,{{r|bultheel}} the [[dimension]]s of spaces, and the possibility of spaces of infinite dimensions, with a mention of [[higher category theory]],{{r|guadarrama}} Cheng's research specialty.{{r|simoson|bultheel}}

The mathematics is frequently lightened and made accessible with personal experiences and stories,{{r|haworth|kean|pw}} involving such subjects as the [[Loch Ness Monster]], [[puff pastry]], boating, dance contests, shoes,{{r|haworth}} "Legos, the iPod Shuffle, snorkeling, Battenberg cakes and Winnie-the-Pooh".{{r|kean}}

==Audience and reception==
The Royal Society judges called ''Beyond Infinity'' "a very engaging introduction to a forbidding subject".{{r|roysoc}} Similarly, reviewer Anne Haworth calls it "engaging  and  readable",{{r|haworth}} and ''[[The Wall Street Journal|Wall Street Journal]]'' reviewer Sam Kean writes that its "chatty tone keeps things fresh".{{r|kean}} It is aimed at a popular audience, not assumed to have a significant background in mathematics, including "the young or those brimming with curiosity"{{r|simoson}} as well as college or secondary-school students,{{r|guadarrama|bultheel}} although it may be "too elementary for mathematicians or mathematics students".{{r|bultheel}}

As similar reading material, reviewer Andrew James Simoson suggests placing this book alongside ''The Book of Numbers'' by [[John Horton Conway]] and [[Richard K. Guy]] (1996), 
''[[One Two Three... Infinity]]'' by [[George Gamow]] (1947), and ''Really Big Numbers'' by [[Richard Schwartz (mathematician)|Richard Schwartz]] (2014).{{r|simoson}}
